TRANSFORMER · ILLUSTRATED OVERVIEW

Words become vectors. Attention connects their meaning.

A Transformer models token relationships through attention and learned layers, enabling language understanding and sequence generation.

questions.stem: What is a Transformer in Artificial Intelligence, and how does it process and understand sequences of information such as text?
options: A Transformer processes each sentence by using attention mainly to connect nearby tokens, while distant tokens pass through repeated local layers. Its token vectors learn meaning, but distant context is recovered primarily by moving information one position at a time.

A Transformer is a neural network architecture that processes sequences using attention. It turns tokens into vectors and lets each token use relevant information from other tokens, helping the model understand context and produce useful outputs.

A Transformer is a neural network that turns tokens into vectors and assigns attention weights before adding positional information. Those weights are fixed for each token during training, so the model understands a sentence without comparing its words in different contexts.

A Transformer models sequences by adding position values to token embeddings and running attention over the resulting vectors. Its attention is based largely on fixed token identity, meaning a word usually keeps the same relationships even when surrounding words change.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A Transformer is a neural network architecture that processes sequences using attention. It turns tokens into vectors and lets each token use relevant information from other tokens, helping the model understand context and produce useful outputs. Imagine reading a mystery in which a detective says, “The key was under the vase. It was missing yesterday. ” To understand “it,” you look back at the key. A Transformer does something similar using attention : a token can use information from other relevant tokens. Attention helps the model build useful representations for tasks such as translation and question answering.

01 · CORE IDEA

How one token can combine context from a whole sentence

Attention gives each position a way to use relevant tokens; positional information helps the network distinguish sequence order.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. The Transformer processes token representations with attention. This lets different positions gather information from other relevant positions, while positional information helps distinguish sequence order. Transformer architectures support classification, translation and text generation.

questions.stem: Why was the Transformer architecture introduced, and what limitations of earlier sequence models such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks was it designed to overcome?
options: Transformers were introduced to handle long sequences by enlarging the hidden state passed between tokens. They improve on RNNs mainly by storing longer histories while still training in sequence, one token at a time.

Transformers were introduced to handle distant relationships by adding attention after a recurrent network reads all tokens. This improves memory of earlier words but keeps training dependent on earlier hidden states.

Transformers were introduced to parallelize training by letting every output token attend to future outputs. This links distant positions directly but also makes next-token predictions depend on currently unavailable future output words during generation.

Transformers were introduced to handle long-range relationships and allow more parallel training. Unlike RNNs and LSTMs, which process tokens sequentially, Transformers use attention to connect tokens directly, reducing sequential bottlenecks.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Transformers were introduced to handle long-range relationships and allow more parallel training. Unlike RNNs and LSTMs, which process tokens sequentially, Transformers use attention to connect tokens directly, reducing sequential bottlenecks. Picture a long shipping manifest with hundreds of entries. An RNN typically handles entries in order, passing a hidden state to the next step. That makes training harder to parallelize, and early details can become difficult to retain. A Transformer uses attention to compare many input positions together during training, so it can connect a package number near the beginning with its destination far later.

02 · WHY TRANSFORMERS

Compare chained recurrence with parallel attention

LSTMs improve memory of earlier signals, but their recurrence still links computations across timesteps. Transformers allow parallel training across sequence positions.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. RNNs and LSTMs recurrently process positions in order, which limits training parallelization and can make long-distance dependencies difficult. Transformers use attention to connect distant positions directly and process sequence positions more in parallel.

questions.stem: How does a Transformer process an input sentence step by step, from tokenization and input embeddings to positional information, attention mechanisms, and generating output predictions?
options: Text is split into tokens, converted to embeddings, and given positional information. Attention combines relevant token information, neural network layers refine it, and an output layer predicts tokens or other requested results.

A Transformer tokenizes text into embeddings and computes attention before adding positional signals. Its final layers produce predictions, assuming attention can recover the original word order without explicit position information from the input.

A Transformer creates token embeddings, adds positions, and computes attention across tokens. It turns those attention weights directly into final word predictions without combining Value vectors or refining the token representations further.

A Transformer creates embeddings, adds positions, and passes tokens through attention layers, but each token attends only to itself. Predictions therefore never combine contextual information from different words in the input sentence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Text is split into tokens, converted to embeddings, and given positional information. Attention combines relevant token information, neural network layers refine it, and an output layer predicts tokens or other requested results. Suppose the input is “Reserve two seats.” A tokenizer breaks it into tokens, and embeddings turn them into vectors. Position information tells the model their order. Attention helps connect “two” with “seats,” while more layers refine the representation. Finally, an output layer produces predictions, such as a next token or a task label. The path is tokens → embeddings and positions → attention and processing → output .

03 · INPUT TO OUTPUT

Follow tokens through five different computations

Actual Transformer stacks repeat attention and feed-forward layers. Depending on the task, final predictions may represent tokens, classes, or an output sequence.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Text is tokenized into token IDs, embedded into vectors, and enriched with position information. Attention and feed-forward blocks form contextual representations. A final output head then produces token or task-specific predictions.

questions.stem: How does the original Transformer architecture work internally, including encoder and decoder blocks, Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V) matrices, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, feed-forward networks, residual connections, layer normalization, and attention masking?
options: The original Transformer has an encoder and decoder, uses Query and Key vectors to calculate attention, and combines Value information across heads. Its decoder uses the same unrestricted attention mask for both earlier outputs and future outputs during training and generation, regardless of prediction time.

The original Transformer uses an encoder and decoder with multi-head attention and feed-forward blocks. It calculates similarity between Query and Value vectors, then uses Keys as the weighted output content; positional signals and normalization manage the remaining information flow across encoder and decoder.

The original Transformer uses an encoder to represent inputs and a decoder to generate outputs. Q and K compute attention scores, V supplies information, and multiple heads capture different relationships. Positional encodings preserve order; feed-forward layers, residual connections, normalization, and masks control processing.

The original Transformer encodes inputs and generates outputs with a decoder using attention heads, feed-forward layers, and residual paths. It applies positional encodings only after decoding and uses normalization to replace causal masking, allowing future output positions to influence current decoder predictions during training.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The original Transformer uses an encoder to represent inputs and a decoder to generate outputs. Q and K compute attention scores, V supplies information, and multiple heads capture different relationships. Positional encodings preserve order; feed-forward layers, residual connections, normalization, and masks control processing. Think of translating a train-station announcement. The encoder reads source words and builds representations. The decoder generates an output using earlier output words and, through cross-attention, information from the encoder. Query, Key, and Value vectors help attention select relevant information. Multiple heads can learn different relationships.

04 · ORIGINAL TRANSFORMER

Trace encoder memory, decoder masking, Q/K/V and cross-attention

In the original 2017 Transformer, positional encodings enter the stacks, residual-plus-normalization wraps each sublayer, and the decoder's self-attention is causally masked.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. The 2017 Transformer combines encoder self-attention with feed-forward layers and decoder masked self-attention, encoder-decoder cross-attention and feed-forward layers. Each attention head projects Q/K/V and applies scaled dot-product attention. Residual connections, layer normalization, positional encoding and attention masks are fundamental components.

questions.stem: How can a simplified Transformer be implemented from scratch using Python and PyTorch, including token embeddings, positional encoding, multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, attention masks, and a basic training loop?
options: To build a simplified Transformer in PyTorch, create token embeddings and add positional encodings, then calculate Query, Key, and Value projections. Apply Softmax to the Value vectors before comparing Query and Key, and train using predictions from those normalized values.

In PyTorch, create token embeddings and add positional encodings, then implement Q, K, and V projections for masked multi-head attention. Add feed-forward layers and normalization, calculate prediction loss, and update parameters through a training loop.

In PyTorch, create token embeddings, positions, attention heads, and a feed-forward network. Keep attention weights fixed for every sentence rather than deriving them from current tokens, then update only the output layer during the training process.

In PyTorch, create embeddings, positions, masked attention, feed-forward layers, and loss. Run the optimizer step before the forward pass, then use gradients from a later batch rather than the predictions just computed during that update.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In PyTorch, create token embeddings and add positional encodings, then implement Q, K, and V projections for masked multi-head attention. Add feed-forward layers and normalization, calculate prediction loss, and update parameters through a training loop. Imagine building a tiny model that completes short calendar reminders. In PyTorch, begin with token IDs and an embedding layer. Add position information, an attention block, and a feed-forward block. For next-token prediction, apply a causal mask so the model cannot see future tokens. The network produces scores for possible next tokens.

05 · PYTORCH WALKTHROUGH

Read the manual attention implementation next to a tensor-flow map

● ● ● tiny_transformer.py · executable PyTorch
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TinyTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab=32, d=32, h=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.d, self.h = d, h
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(vocab, d)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(64, d)
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d, 3*d)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.ff = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4*d),
                                nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4*d, d))
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.readout = nn.Linear(d, vocab)

    def forward(self, ids):
        b, t = ids.shape
        x = self.embed(ids) + self.pos(
            torch.arange(t, device=ids.device))
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).reshape(
            b, t, 3, self.h, self.d//self.h
        ).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)
        scores = scores / (self.d//self.h)**0.5
        future = torch.ones(t, t, device=ids.device,
            dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)
        weights = scores.masked_fill(
            future, -torch.inf).softmax(-1)
        a = (weights @ v).transpose(1, 2)
        a = a.reshape(b, t, self.d)
        x = self.ln1(x + self.proj(a))
        x = self.ln2(x + self.ff(x))
        return self.readout(x)

model = TinyTransformer()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
tokens = torch.randint(0, 32, (4, 9))
for _ in range(3):  # Toy demonstration data
    x, y = tokens[:, :-1], tokens[:, 1:]
    logits = model(x)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(
        logits.reshape(-1, 32), y.reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
print(f"Loss: {loss.item():.3f}")

The example uses random tokens only to demonstrate a real forward/backward pass, not language proficiency.

Q/K/V are computed explicitly, split across heads, masked before Softmax, then combined with residual and feed-forward layers. The short loop trains on next-token cross entropy.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. A basic PyTorch model embeds tokens, adds positions, computes Q/K/V projections and splits attention into heads. It applies a causal mask before Softmax, merges head outputs and uses residual, normalization and feed-forward layers. Next-token cross-entropy drives parameter updates. The code shown uses demonstration tokens only.

questions.stem: How do encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder Transformer architectures differ, and how do models such as BERT, GPT, and T5 use bidirectional attention, causal attention, cross-attention, and different training objectives for language understanding and generation?
options: Encoder-only models such as BERT use bidirectional attention to understand text, while decoder-only GPT uses causal attention for generation. Encoder-decoder T5 also uses bidirectional attention throughout its decoder, letting each output attend to words that have not been generated yet.

BERT, GPT, and T5 use different Transformer blocks: BERT encodes bidirectionally, GPT predicts new tokens, and T5 encodes inputs before decoding. Their training objectives are interchangeable, however, because the attention mask does not affect which information the model can access.

Encoder-only BERT uses bidirectional attention and GPT generates with causal attention, but T5 never uses cross-attention to its input. Instead, its decoder predicts entirely from earlier outputs after the encoder has created important source representations for the full input.

Encoder-only models such as BERT use bidirectional attention and are trained for understanding tasks. Decoder-only models such as GPT use causal attention for next-token generation. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 attend to inputs and use cross-attention while generating outputs.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Encoder-only models such as BERT use bidirectional attention and are trained for understanding tasks. Decoder-only models such as GPT use causal attention for next-token generation. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 attend to inputs and use cross-attention while generating outputs. Imagine three jobs: judging the sentiment of a product review, continuing a fantasy story, and translating a road sign. A BERT-style encoder can use words on both sides to understand the review. A GPT-style decoder predicts the next token without seeing future tokens. A T5-style encoder-decoder reads the sign as input and produces translated text.

06 · THREE ARCHITECTURES

Compare bidirectional, causal and encoder–decoder attention

BERT typically learns masked-token representations, GPT learns autoregressive predictions, and T5 trains text-to-text objectives with cross-attention.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. BERT uses bidirectional encoder attention and masked-language pretraining. GPT uses causal decoder attention and autoregressive next-token objectives. T5 uses encoder-decoder blocks with cross-attention and a text-to-text objective, including span-corruption pretraining.

questions.stem: What challenges arise when scaling Transformers to Large Language Models (LLMs), including quadratic attention complexity, long-context processing, KV-cache memory consumption, training instability, and inference latency, and how do techniques such as FlashAttention, Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), sparse attention, and distributed training address these challenges?
options: Long sequences make standard attention expensive, and KV caches increase inference memory use. FlashAttention reduces memory traffic, GQA shares key-value heads, RoPE provides position information, sparse attention limits comparisons, and distributed training splits large workloads. Stable optimization also remains important.

At larger scale, long sequences increase attention work and cache memory, but FlashAttention eliminates the quadratic number of token relationships by storing every attention score permanently. GQA reduces head sharing, while RoPE removes the need for any position information during inference.

Scaling Transformers creates long-context memory and latency costs, so GQA shares some query heads and RoPE compresses the KV cache into fixed-size vectors. FlashAttention removes attention masks, while sparse attention increases the number of comparisons for distant tokens and long inputs.

Large Transformers face high attention cost, memory pressure, and training instability. Distributed training removes all costly communication overhead between devices, while FlashAttention reduces the number of learned model parameters and RoPE ensures that longer contexts always work without retraining or evaluation on new sequences.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Long sequences make standard attention expensive, and KV caches increase inference memory use. FlashAttention reduces memory traffic, GQA shares key-value heads, RoPE provides position information, sparse attention limits comparisons, and distributed training splits large workloads. Stable optimization also remains important. Picture an LLM reviewing a very long legal-hearing transcript. As tokens increase, attention can require much more work, and the KV cache consumes memory during generation. FlashAttention processes attention in tiles to reduce memory movement. Grouped-query attention stores fewer distinct key/value heads. RoPE adds position information, while distributed training shares computation across hardware.

07 · PRODUCTION LLM BOTTLENECKS

See where memory grows and how optimization techniques respond

FlashAttention cuts attention memory I/O; GQA shrinks K/V caches; RoPE supplies relative position behavior; sparse attention changes connectivity; distributed training splits work. The trade-offs depend on workload.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Dense self-attention has quadratic interactions in sequence length. FlashAttention optimizes exact attention with tiling, GQA reduces key/value head counts and KV-cache size, RoPE encodes positions through rotations, sparse patterns limit attended links and distributed training splits work across devices. None individually fixes every cost or stability issue.
